strengths: The core insight is simple, intuitive, and technically sound: transitioning from standard global linear (scale-and-shift) depth transformation to a radar-conditioned polynomial transformation enables non-uniform, depth-dependent corrections to rectify inter-object relative depth discrepancies in monocular depth estimates.

The proposed monotonicity regularization via the first derivative of the polynomial transformation provides an effective inductive bias that mitigates polynomial oscillations and maintains intra-object ordinality.

The paper provides strong empirical performance across three diverse radar-camera depth estimation benchmarks (nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, and View-of-Delft), consistently and significantly outperforming existing methods across multiple evaluation ranges.

The experimental validation is thorough, including comprehensive comparisons across multiple MDE foundation backbones (UniDepth, Depth Anything, Depth Pro, DPT), polynomial degree sensitivity analysis, and ablations on network components.
weaknesses: The polynomial transformation is strictly a 1D mapping $f: z \mapsto \hat{d}$ applied globally across the entire frame. Consequently, while it can resolve depth-dependent misalignments between objects situated at different predicted depths, it cannot correct spatial misalignments between objects or regions that have the same or similar initial predicted MDE depth $z$. Discussing this theoretical limitation would clarify the scope of the method.

The monotonicity loss penalizes $|1 - d\hat{d}/dz|$. Encouraging the derivative to be close to 1 implicitly assumes that the input scaleless depth $z$ is already roughly on a metric scale (e.g., from UniDepth/Depth Pro). For inverse depth or arbitrary relative depth backbones (like DPT / Depth Anything), the expected slope may differ significantly from 1 unless an explicit normalization or pre-scaling step is applied; the paper should provide clearer implementation details on how $z$ is normalized before this regularizer is enforced.

While the computational overhead of polynomial evaluation is claimed to be negligible, the main paper lacks explicit inference runtime, latency, or FLOPs comparisons relative to competing radar-camera baselines.

strengths: The core conceptual insight—extending global scale-and-shift alignment to polynomial fitting to correct inter-region/inter-object depth misalignments in monocular depth estimation (MDE) models—is intuitive, elegant, and well-motivated.

The proposed monotonicity regularization via first-derivative penalization (|1 - d(d_hat)/dz|) is a technically sound mechanism to prevent polynomial oscillations and depth ordering inversions that typically plague higher-degree polynomial regression.

Extensive experimental evaluation across three public radar-camera benchmarks (nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, and View-of-Delft) demonstrating clear, consistent quantitative and qualitative improvements over existing radar-depth completion/fusion baselines.

Thorough analysis and ablation studies examining the sensitivity to polynomial degree, choice of foundation MDE backbone (DPT, Depth Anything, Depth Pro, UniDepth), and key architectural components (radar prototypes, cross-attention fusion, and monotonicity loss).
weaknesses: Missing details on numerical normalization: High-order polynomial evaluation (up to degree 8 or 10) on raw depth values (up to 80m) can lead to severe numerical instability or gradient explosion unless the scaleless input depth z is normalized (e.g., to [0, 1]). The paper should clearly specify how z and the polynomial basis are scaled and numerically conditioned.

Assumption of a globally uniform mapping function: PolyRad learns a single global polynomial transformation across the entire image via global average pooling. While this resolves depth-dependent misalignments, it cannot correct spatially varying distortions (e.g., peripheral distortion or pitch/height-dependent scale drift) where pixels with the same initial depth z require different metric corrections.

Over-constraining derivative regularization: Enforcing the derivative d(d_hat)/dz to be strictly close to 1 in Eq. (8) implies an identity mapping slope. For scaleless MDEs whose outputs may have an arbitrary arbitrary median scale (e.g., Depth Anything / DPT before rescaling), this term may overly penalize legitimate global scaling factors different from 1.

strengths: Principled and well-motivated formulation: The paper clearly identifies the limitation of standard linear (scale-and-shift) depth alignment when monocular depth estimators exhibit non-uniform relative errors across multiple depth ranges, while also avoiding the severely ill-posed nature of per-pixel depth completion from sparse radar data.

Effective regularization for polynomial stability: Incorporating a first-derivative regularization term into the training objective provides an elegant and computationally lightweight way to enforce local monotonicity and prevent oscillatory behavior commonly associated with higher-degree polynomial fitting.

Strong and consistent empirical performance: PolyRad achieves substantial improvements in MAE and RMSE across three major automotive datasets (nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, and View-of-Delft) over competitive baselines such as RadarCam-Depth and GET-UP.

Comprehensive experimental validation: The authors evaluate multiple monocular depth estimation backbones (DPT, Depth Anything, Depth Pro, UniDepth), provide a systematic sweep of the polynomial degree hyperparameter, and conduct clear ablations on architectural components (radar prototypes, cross-attention, monotonicity loss).
weaknesses: Rigidity of global 1D mapping: The polynomial transformation operates purely as a 1D mapping applied uniformly across all image pixels based solely on their scaleless depth value z. Consequently, if the monocular depth model makes spatially dependent errors (e.g., predicting different relative depths for two objects at identical metric distances on opposite sides of the frame), a global polynomial cannot resolve them without introducing errors elsewhere.

Monotonicity regularization loss design: The loss term penalizes |1 - d(d_hat)/dz|, which encourages the first derivative to remain close to 1. While this guarantees positivity (and hence monotonicity), it also penalizes legitimate global scale expansion or compression (i.e., slopes significantly different from 1). A non-negativity penalty (such as ReLU(-d(d_hat)/dz)) combined with data supervision would be more theoretically aligned with enforcing monotonicity without constraining the scale.

Limited investigation into radar elevation ambiguity and noise: mmWave radar suffers heavily from elevation angle ambiguity and multipath clutter. While learnable prototypes are claimed to filter these nuisances, there is limited quantitative analysis or ablation isolating prototype behavior against varying levels of radar sparsity and artificial noise.

strengths: Principled and practical perspective: Framing metric depth recovery from MDE foundation models and sparse radar as a parameter-efficient polynomial fitting problem is an insightful middle ground between rigid 2-parameter affine transformations and unconstrained, ill-posed per-pixel dense regression.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The proposed POLAR method demonstrates solid gains over existing radar-camera depth completion and fusion methods (such as RadarCam-Depth, GET-UP, and TacoDepth) across three widely used autonomous driving benchmarks (nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, and View-of-Delft).

High computational efficiency: Predicting global polynomial coefficients bypasses heavy dense fusion decoders, achieving >40 FPS inference speed and significantly reduced FLOPs compared to recent state-of-the-art baselines.

Thorough ablation and comparative studies: The paper provides extensive experiments exploring polynomial degrees, prototype clustering, zero-shot cross-dataset generalization, robustness under reduced radar point densities, and alternative regression/adapter baselines.
weaknesses: Spatially invariant transfer function limitation: The polynomial coefficients are predicted once per scene, meaning the mapping $\hat{d} = f(z)$ is a global 1D transfer function. While it introduces non-linear curvature along the depth range, it cannot resolve spatial ambiguities where two distinct objects share identical initial MDE depth $z$ but require different metric adjustments. The text occasionally conflates non-linear 1D re-scaling with correcting arbitrary cross-region spatial misalignments.

Formulation of the monotonicity loss: The proposed monotonicity regularizer in Eq. (6) penalizes $\| 1_{H\times W} - d\hat{d}/dz \|_1$, explicitly biasing the derivative toward 1. This is significantly more restrictive than enforcing non-negativity (i.e., $\max(0, -d\hat{d}/dz)$), and inherently biases the transformation toward the identity slope $\hat{d} \approx z + c$. The justification for choosing a target derivative of 1 rather than standard one-sided penalty terms should be clarified, especially when input scaleless depth scales differ significantly from metric ranges.

Superficial theoretical formalization: Proposition 1 and its proof (Appendix H) formally demonstrate that three non-collinear points cannot be fitted by a 2D straight line. Presenting basic elementary geometry as a formal theoretical proposition feels somewhat overstated and adds little technical depth beyond the intuitive geometric argument already made in Section 3.1.

strengths: Compelling and intuitive core motivation: Moving beyond standard affine (scale-and-shift) alignment to a low-degree polynomial mapping is an elegant, well-grounded formulation that effectively addresses non-linear depth distortions across different ranges without suffering from the high degrees of freedom of pixel-level dense decoders.

Effective regularization: Enforcing monotonicity via first-derivative regularization (|1 - d(d_hat)/dz|) is a neat and practical mechanism to prevent the oscillatory and overfitting behaviors (e.g., Runge's phenomenon / order inversions) typically associated with higher-degree polynomial fitting.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Evaluated across three public multi-modal driving datasets (nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, View-of-Delft) against recent state-of-the-art radar-camera baselines (TacoDepth, RadarCam-Depth, GET-UP), consistently demonstrating superior MAE and RMSE across 50m, 70m, and 80m cutoffs.

Strong computational efficiency: By predicting only N+1 global coefficients rather than decoding high-resolution feature maps, POLAR achieves real-time inference (24.81 ms / ~40.3 fps) and low computational overhead (89.7 GFLOPs), outperforming heavy fusion baselines in both speed and memory footprint.

Thorough ablations and diagnostics: The paper includes extensive studies on polynomial degrees, feature aggregation choices, zero-shot cross-dataset transfer, robustness to downsampled radar point clouds, and comparisons against 1D regression methods (PCHIP, Isotonic) and PEFT adapters.
weaknesses: Formulation of the monotonicity loss: The term ||1_{H x W} - d(d_hat)/dz||_1 penalizes deviations from a unit derivative (d(d_hat)/dz = 1). If the input scaleless depth z is arbitrary in magnitude or normalized to [0, 1] while ground truth d_gt is in meters (0 to 80m), the true derivative scale should be significantly different from 1. The paper does not sufficiently clarify whether z is pre-scaled or why targeting exactly 1 is preferred over an isotonic penalty (e.g., ReLU(-d(d_hat)/dz)) or a data-dependent scale.

Inherent limitation of global 1D polynomial mapping: Because the mapping d_hat = f(z) is globally applied to all pixels purely based on their scalar value z, any two pixels sharing identical MDE predictions z must map to identical metric depth d_hat, regardless of their 2D image coordinates or local radar measurements. While this parameter efficiency prevents overfitting to sparse radar points, the paper should explicitly discuss this trade-off regarding spatially varying MDE distortion.

Triviality in Proposition 1 (Appendix H): Proposition 1 proves that there exist 3 points that cannot be fit by a single line in 2D. Formalizing the fact that three non-collinear points cannot be fit by an affine line as a 'Proposition' with a proof by contradiction is mathematically elementary and overcomplicates an otherwise clear geometric intuition.

Minor presentation inconsistencies: There are minor numerical discrepancies across the text when citing overall percentage improvements (e.g., Abstract states 24.9% MAE / 33.2% RMSE, Introduction states 29.1% average, and Section 4.1 breaks down individual datasets).

strengths: Insightful and refreshing formulation: Instead of relying on heavy pixel-wise decoders or adhering strictly to the common affine (scale-and-shift) assumption, the paper proposes a radar-conditioned polynomial fitting framework to adapt scaleless monocular depth estimation (MDE) predictions into metric depth.

Comprehensive empirical validation: POLAR achieves consistent and solid state-of-the-art results across three challenging automotive radar benchmarks (nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, and View-of-Delft), substantially outperforming recent baselines such as RadarCam-Depth and TacoDepth.

Remarkable computational efficiency: By predicting only a compact set of polynomial coefficients via aggregated prototype-guided radar-MDE features, the inference overhead is minimal (24.8 ms / ~40.3 fps and 89.7 GFLOPs), making it well-suited for real-time robotic and automotive deployment.

Effective regularization for stability: Addressing the risk of overfitting and non-monotonic oscillations associated with higher-degree polynomials via a first-derivative regularization term is well-motivated, and its effectiveness is validated quantitatively using rank correlation (Kendall's tau).

Thorough ablations and analysis: The paper provides thorough explorations across different MDE backbones (UniDepth, Depth Anything, Depth Pro, DPT), polynomial degree sensitivity, zero-shot cross-dataset generalization, and robustness to reduced radar point densities.
weaknesses: Fundamental limitation of a spatially invariant 1D transfer function: Because the polynomial mapping d = sum(c_i * z^i) operates solely on the scalar depth value z, it is globally applied across the entire image. If two distinct objects or regions share similar initial MDE depth values but require distinct metric adjustments, a global 1D polynomial cannot separate them. The paper occasionally overclaims spatial adaptability (e.g., 'sharpening fine object boundaries'), whereas the polynomial can only stretch or compress specific depth intervals globally.

Formulation of the monotonicity loss: Eq. (6) penalizes ||1 - d(d_hat)/dz||_1, which directly drives the derivative toward 1 (identity slope). While this prevents oscillations, it actually enforces an identity-like slope rather than strictly enforcing monotonicity (d(d_hat)/dz > 0). An asymmetric barrier or hinge loss (e.g., penalizing only negative derivatives) would theoretically be more faithful to the stated goal of isotonic/monotonic ordering. A discussion or comparison regarding this design choice is lacking.

Over-formalization of trivial properties: Section 3.1 and Proposition 1 (Appendix H) dedicate formal proofs and propositions to establish that three generic points in R^2 cannot be fitted exactly by an affine line. This is an elementary property of linear systems and does not require formal 'proof by construction'; framing it as a theoretical contribution slightly detracts from the presentation.

Sensitivity to polynomial degree: As demonstrated in Table 5, performance peaks around degree 8 and degrades at degree 10 due to high-degree instability. The method requires careful hyperparameter tuning of the degree N per dataset, which may hinder out-of-the-box generalization to novel environments.
